finding: In 50 periodontal surgery patients, binaural-beat exposure was associated with lower postoperative anxiety and physiological stress measures than no auditory intervention. Mean anxiety scores in the intervention arm fell from 49.0 to 38.7.
limitation: The comparison did not control for music, headphones or attention. A small surgical study does not establish a general clinical effect of binaural beats.

finding: In 72 surgical patients, 30 minutes of 1 Hz binaural beats reduced the mean remimazolam dose required for loss of consciousness from 17.7 to 15.0 mg; hypotension occurred in 6% versus 28% of participants.
limitation: A single-centre anaesthesia study with no auditory intervention in the comparison arm. EEG differences were not significant, so the proposed entrainment mechanism remains unconfirmed.

finding: Preoperative binaural-beat stimulation produced a greater reduction in reported state anxiety than the control condition. The reported difference in relative anxiety change was approximately six percentage points.
limitation: The authors identified music and relaxation as plausible contributors. Alpha power did not differ between groups; the trial does not isolate a beat-specific mechanism.

finding: Among 69 surgical patients, 20 minutes of 1 Hz binaural beats reduced the mean propofol dose needed to stop responding to verbal commands from 105 to 87 mg; the difference was -18 mg, with a 95% confidence interval of -32 to -5 mg.
limitation: Anxiety and frontal EEG bands did not differ significantly. This supports an anaesthetic-dose finding within the tested clinical protocol, rather than a general claim of brainwave entrainment.

finding: In 52 completers, theta-range binaural stimulation with pink noise after cycling increased prefrontal theta and alpha EEG power relative to sham stimulation.
limitation: This was an immediate physiological experiment in healthy adults. It did not establish improved recovery, cognition or a clinical treatment effect; 60 people were recruited.

finding: A pilot involving 30 people with multiple sclerosis and 30 healthy participants reported lower salivary cortisol after 4 Hz binaural stimulation than sham following an experimental stress challenge, alongside autonomic and EEG changes.
limitation: Small, mixed participant groups and acute follow-up limit generalisation. Cortisol is a hormonal biomarker; this study did not measure gene expression or demonstrate long-term clinical benefit.

finding: In 96 patients undergoing unsedated upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, binaural-beat music was associated with improved anxiety, procedure tolerance and satisfaction compared with no intervention.
limitation: The trial did not include an otherwise identical music control, so the contribution of the beats is unresolved. Blood pressure and heart rate did not differ significantly.

finding: In 49 boys undergoing surgery with a caudal block, audiovisual brainwave entrainment reduced the median propofol infusion requirement from 4.2 to 3.0 mg/kg/hour.
limitation: The intervention combined sound and visual stimulation and cannot establish an isolated binaural-beat effect. Findings concern supervised paediatric anaesthesia, not unsupervised sedation or general wellbeing.

finding: A 61-person cataract-surgery trial reported lower operative pain, anxiety and heart rate with binaural-beat audio than with silent headphones.
limitation: A small procedure-specific study with a silence comparator. It does not separate beat effects from the effects of hearing calming audio.

finding: Among 64 older adults with poor sleep in long-term care, binaural beats embedded in familiar music improved sleep measures and selected autonomic measures relative to the same music without beats over 14 days.
limitation: The short intervention and single institutional setting limit inference about durable sleep improvement. Physiological changes do not establish a molecular mechanism.

finding: A sham-controlled crossover study reported lower pain ratings and analgesic use after 5 Hz binaural stimulation in people with chronic pain, together with increased EEG power at the stimulation frequency.
limitation: Sample size and participant flow require full-text appraisal. The short treatment periods and crossover design limit conclusions about sustained benefit or wider patient populations.

finding: In men undergoing cystoscopy or ureteral stent removal, binaural beats reduced pain compared with classical music and silent headphones; both sound interventions improved anxiety relative to silence.
limitation: The analysed procedure groups totalled 352 participants after exclusions. Procedure tolerance was less favourable with binaural beats, and results are specific to these urological settings.

finding: In 40 older adults undergoing knee replacement, preoperative 4 Hz binaural beats reduced first-day self-administered morphine from 11.85 to 5.75 mg compared with matched tones presented at the same frequency to both ears.
limitation: Pain ratings did not differ between groups. This small, single-centre trial supports an opioid-consumption finding in a specific surgical protocol, with broader effectiveness still requiring replication.

finding: In 99 root-canal patients, binaural beats and 432 Hz music each reduced preoperative anxiety relative to white noise. Participants and outcome assessors were described as blinded.
limitation: The two active audio conditions did not differ significantly. The trial does not demonstrate a unique therapeutic property of 432 Hz or superiority of binaural beats over music.

finding: In 60 orthodontic patients, alpha binaural-beat music reduced several pain measures late in the first week after appliance placement relative to no music.
limitation: Pain did not differ between binaural-beat music and otherwise similar music without beats. The successful audio experience does not establish an additional beat-specific benefit.

finding: Among 112 bronchoscopy patients, the binaural-music arm showed a larger numerical reduction in state anxiety than plain music or no music, with reductions in blood pressure.
limitation: The abstract mainly reports within-group changes, so those numbers alone do not establish superiority over plain music. The trial was retrospectively registered.

finding: A 252-child dental trial reported reduced preoperative fear, anxiety and physiological arousal with device-based brainwave entrainment compared with standard behaviour management.
limitation: The device combines stimulation components. The abstract does not establish a binaural-beat-only effect, and masking, allocation and registration timing require full-text appraisal.

finding: In 84 women with fibromyalgia, eight weeks of headset-based brainwave entrainment produced improvements in pain and anxiety, with changes in quality of life, oxidative stress and circulating BDNF also examined.
limitation: Music therapy improved several outcomes as well. The abstract does not provide a consistent set of between-group effect estimates; the mixed headset intervention and protein measurements do not establish a gene-expression mechanism.

finding: Among 27 stroke rehabilitation completers, the binaural-stimulation group improved daily-living and depression scores more than the music comparison group. Balance measures improved in both groups.
limitation: The small sample and combined rehabilitation context limit causal attribution to the beats. Correlations between functional measures do not prove a brain mechanism.

finding: In 31 healthy participants, brief 10 Hz binaural stimulation improved selected visuospatial response-speed and stability measures during a working-memory task.
limitation: Effects were small and differed across sensory modalities; auditory-verbal measures did not show the same pattern. There were 155 condition sessions, not 155 independent participants, and no clinical outcome was tested.

finding: Of 151 women randomised after a traumatic birth, 143 entered the reported intention-to-treat analysis. Two early postpartum EMDR sessions reduced self-reported and clinician-rated PTSD symptom severity compared with two telephone contacts; the reported raw symptom differences were 8.7 and 3.8 points respectively.
limitation: Clinician-diagnosed PTSD rates did not differ significantly. The abstract contains an inconsistent confidence-interval entry, so that interval is not reproduced here; follow-up was nine weeks postpartum.

finding: In 159 people with personality disorders, EMDR reduced PTSD symptoms more than a waitlist. Among participants with PTSD receiving EMDR, 65.5% no longer met the diagnosis after treatment and 73.1% at follow-up.
limitation: A waitlist does not control for therapeutic attention. The remission percentages describe the treated subgroup; they are not an absolute treatment effect or a general remission guarantee.

finding: In 24 forensic patients with psychosis and PTSD, blinded assessments favoured EMDR over routine-care waitlist for clinician-rated PTSD symptoms. The estimated difference averaged across follow-ups was 11.4 points, with a 95% confidence interval of 1.3 to 21.4.
limitation: Recruitment was curtailed by pandemic restrictions, leaving a small sample. Psychotic symptoms and adverse events did not differ significantly, so effectiveness claims remain specific to the measured PTSD outcomes.

finding: In 120 women exposed to violence, ten sessions of EMDR produced greater reported improvements in post-traumatic symptoms, anxiety, depression, quality of life and selected cognitive tests than narrative exposure therapy.
limitation: The abstract supplies significance levels without effect-size confidence intervals. Masking, multiple comparisons and durability require further appraisal before a high-confidence comparative claim.

finding: The 40-person EMERALD trial in critical-illness survivors achieved 98% clinician-rated follow-up at 12 months. Exploratory PTSD symptom change favoured EMDR plus usual care by 14.1 points, with a 95% confidence interval of 6.2 to 22.0 points.
limitation: Feasibility, acceptability and safety were the primary objectives. The symptom estimate is hypothesis-generating and does not establish definitive treatment effectiveness.

finding: A 38-person pilot found greater reductions in binge-eating symptoms, days and frequency with an adapted ten-session EMDR protocol than waitlist, alongside improvements in selected anxiety and sleep outcomes.
limitation: Treatment completion was 68.8%, and several other outcomes did not improve. The small pilot and immediate post-treatment assessment support a larger trial rather than a settled treatment recommendation.

finding: In 60 early-psychosis service users, a 16-session EMDR adaptation met trial feasibility targets and showed promising clinical signals at six months. PTSD symptoms and general-health signals remained evident at 12 months.
limitation: The study was designed to establish feasibility. Follow-up completion was 70% at 12 months, and the efficacy signals require confirmation in a larger trial.

finding: In 22 treatment-resistant depression inpatients, both EMDR and trauma-focused CBT improved depressive symptoms; a post-hoc comparison favoured EMDR at the 12-week follow-up.
limitation: The small pilot and post-hoc nature of the comparison limit confidence in superiority. Benefits were only partly maintained at 24 weeks.

finding: In 20 people with bipolar disorder and trauma histories, EMDR improved depressive, hypomanic and trauma symptoms relative to usual care after treatment, using blinded outcome ratings.
limitation: The trial was small, with unequal dropout between groups. Most differences were not sustained at the 24-week assessment; this is an adjunctive pilot rather than evidence for replacing established bipolar treatment.

design: Single-blind randomized controlled trial (outcome assessors blinded)
finding: A 155-person international trial found substantial PTSD improvement after either EMDR or imagery rescripting for childhood-related trauma, with a 7.7% dropout rate.
limitation: The active treatments did not differ significantly. This supports EMDR as a promising structured treatment in this population, without establishing superiority to imagery rescripting.

finding: In 140 people with PTSD, EMDR and brief eclectic psychotherapy produced similar final improvements; EMDR achieved improvement more rapidly during treatment.
limitation: Dropout was substantial in both groups, approximately 29% and 36%. Faster improvement does not establish superior final outcomes or effectiveness of an automated EMDR-derived intervention.

design: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial
finding: Among 114 participants in the IREM childhood-trauma trial, both EMDR and imagery rescripting improved adaptive and maladaptive schema-mode measures, with gains maintained to one year.
limitation: This is a secondary publication from the same trial as PMID 32892758, not an independent replication. The two treatments did not differ significantly on these outcomes.

finding: An eight-week workplace mindfulness study, with 25 meditators and 16 waitlist participants tested, reported greater left-anterior EEG activation and a stronger influenza-vaccine antibody response in the meditation group.
limitation: Small sample, waitlist comparator and physiological endpoints limit clinical inference. Antibody response and EEG activity are not measurements of gene expression.

finding: Among 90 cancer outpatients completing a seven-week mindfulness programme, mood disturbance and stress symptoms improved relative to waitlist; the intervention group reported reductions of 65% and 31% respectively.
limitation: Those percentages describe change within the treated group, not the between-group treatment effect. The heterogeneous cancer population and waitlist comparison limit specificity.

finding: In 84 breast-cancer survivors, six weeks of adapted MBSR improved depression, anxiety, fear of recurrence and selected quality-of-life measures relative to usual care.
limitation: The assessment was short-term and the comparator did not match treatment attention. The study concerns survivorship wellbeing, not tumour response or cancer prevention.

finding: In 49 older adults with sleep disturbance, mindful-awareness training improved Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores by 1.8 points more than structured sleep-hygiene education, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.6 to 2.9.
limitation: The trial was small and measured immediate post-treatment effects. Inflammatory NF-kappaB measures did not differ between groups, so the sleep benefit does not establish that molecular pathway as its cause.

finding: In a 93-person generalised-anxiety trial, MBSR improved several secondary anxiety ratings and stress-challenge responses more than stress-management education.
limitation: The primary Hamilton Anxiety outcome improved in both arms without a significant between-group difference. The positive findings are secondary outcomes and laboratory stress responses.

finding: In 150 people with multiple sclerosis, eight weeks of mindfulness training improved nonphysical quality of life, depression and fatigue relative to usual care, with benefits persisting at six months.
limitation: The comparison did not control for instructor attention, and outcomes concerned wellbeing rather than disease progression. The paper classifies its evidence as Class III.

finding: In 229 breast-cancer survivors, eight-week MBSR improved mood, breast- and endocrine-related quality of life and wellbeing relative to standard care, with several benefits retained at 12 weeks.
limitation: A waitlist-style standard-care comparison leaves nonspecific support effects unresolved. These are supportive-care outcomes rather than evidence of anticancer activity.

finding: In an 88-person smoking-cessation trial, mindfulness training reduced smoking more than the comparison programme; carbon-monoxide-confirmed seven-day abstinence at week 17 was 31% versus 6%.
limitation: The end-of-treatment abstinence difference was not statistically significant. This was an initial, small trial with a relatively short follow-up.

design: Single-blind randomized controlled trial (outcome assessors blinded)
finding: In the 616-student Mindful Student Study, an eight-week course reduced exam-period psychological distress relative to usual support. The adjusted difference was -0.14 CORE-OM points, with a 95% confidence interval of -0.22 to -0.06.
limitation: Only 74% completed the exam-period outcome, and 59% of assigned students attended at least half the course. Participants knew allocation and the comparator did not match instructor attention.

finding: In 286 adults completing substance-use treatment, mindfulness-based relapse prevention reduced substance-use days and heavy drinking at 12 months relative to standard relapse prevention and usual aftercare.
limitation: Benefits varied by endpoint and time: standard relapse prevention delayed first drug use more effectively at six months. Results concern structured aftercare, not a stand-alone meditation cure for addiction.

finding: In a 73-person recurrent-depression trial, MBCT reduced relapse among the 55 participants with three or more prior episodes: 36% relapsed versus 78% with usual care.
limitation: The 18-person subgroup with two prior episodes showed the opposite numerical pattern. The successful result applies to the specified recurrent-depression subgroup and cannot be generalised across all depression histories.

finding: In 75 healthy volunteers, brief mindfulness training reduced experimentally induced pain more than placebo conditioning or sham mindfulness, with different associated brain-activation patterns.
limitation: An acute laboratory pain experiment does not establish durable benefit for chronic pain. Neuroimaging associations do not identify a single exclusive therapeutic mechanism.

design: Single-blind randomized controlled trial (outcome assessors blinded)
finding: A two-site trial in 173 veterans found greater clinician-rated PTSD improvement with an eight-week mantram programme than present-centred therapy; the between-group CAPS difference was approximately ten points. Insomnia also improved.
limitation: Participants knew the intervention received. Not every responder measure differed, and results apply to taught mantram practice rather than passive or sub-audible delivery.

finding: Among 93 adults living with HIV, mantram repetition improved trait anger and selected spiritual-wellbeing measures relative to an attention-control programme.
limitation: Benefits were outcome-specific. Associations between practice frequency and improvement are observational within the trial and do not establish a dose-response effect or an HIV disease-modifying benefit.

finding: A small mantram study in combat veterans reported promising effects on PTSD symptoms, distress and quality of life, with 29 of 33 enrolled participants completing the study.
limitation: This feasibility study used a delayed-treatment comparison and imprecise small-sample estimates. It provides a development signal rather than definitive clinical effectiveness evidence.

design: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial
finding: In a 146-veteran trial, adding mantram repetition to usual care increased mindful attention; changes in mindful attention statistically mediated improvements in PTSD symptoms, depression and wellbeing.
limitation: This is a secondary mechanistic analysis of the underlying trial. Statistical mediation does not prove the causal mechanism, and the comparison did not isolate attention or expectancy effects.

design: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial
finding: In the 173-veteran mantram trial, hyperarousal improved more than with nonspecific psychotherapy, with effect sizes of 0.57 after treatment and 0.52 at follow-up.
limitation: This reuses the cohort reported in PMID 29921143 and is not an independent replication. Mediation analyses support a hypothesis about hyperarousal, not proof of an exclusive mechanism.

finding: A 26-person internet mantram pilot in breast-cancer survivors established delivery feasibility and reported exploratory changes in stress, spiritual wellbeing and selected serum cytokines.
limitation: Clinical and cytokine outcomes were secondary. Pooled pre/post stress changes do not establish a randomised between-group effect; the small cytokine subset requires replication and measured proteins rather than gene expression.

design: Single-blind randomized controlled trial (outcome assessors blinded)
finding: A trial enrolling 127 older Black adults with hypertension found greater three-month blood-pressure reductions with Transcendental Meditation than progressive muscle relaxation or health education, using blinded blood-pressure observers.
limitation: Sixteen participants were lost to follow-up. The older, short-duration trial does not establish sustained cardiovascular-event reduction or replacement of antihypertensive care.

finding: In 22 veterans receiving MBSR, responders showed increased FKBP5 methylation while nonresponders showed decreased methylation, following the corrected direction reported in the 2021 corrigendum.
limitation: The exploratory responder comparison was not randomised; its multiplicity-adjusted p value was 0.052. SLC6A4 did not show a corresponding positive result. Blood DNA methylation is distinct from brain gene expression.

finding: An eight-day meditation retreat study reported coordinated blood-transcriptome changes in immune-related genes, including interferon-associated pathways, providing a candidate molecular signature for further testing.
limitation: The intensive retreat lacked a randomised control and combined multiple lifestyle changes. Expression changes do not establish improved antiviral protection or clinical treatment efficacy.

design: Gene-expression dataset from a randomized trial
finding: A blood gene-expression dataset from 60 older adults with mild cognitive impairment compares mindful-awareness practice with health education over nine months. It provides a reusable resource for analysing intervention-associated molecular patterns.
limitation: This is a data publication, not independent proof of a successful clinical or molecular effect. Participant overlap with associated trial reports must be retained in any synthesis.

finding: In 60 glaucoma patients, a three-week meditation adjunct reduced intraocular pressure relative to medication alone and was associated with trabecular-meshwork expression changes involving nitric-oxide and inflammatory pathways.
limitation: The measured tissue was ocular rather than brain tissue. The short, small trial and multiple molecular endpoints do not establish a general genomic mechanism or replacement for glaucoma care.

finding: In 90 patients with primary open-angle glaucoma, a short mindfulness programme reduced intraocular pressure relative to waitlist and reported associated stress-biomarker and gene-expression changes.
limitation: A small, short-duration adjunctive trial with a waitlist comparator. Expression and biomarker associations do not prove mediation of pressure reduction or broad effects across diseases.

design: Exploratory genetic analysis of a randomized trial
finding: In 128 breast-cancer survivors randomised to MBSR or education/support, variants including DRD2 rs6277 were associated with differences in cognitive response to the intervention.
limitation: This was a small exploratory moderator analysis across multiple variants. It measured genotype, not altered gene expression, and is not a validated genetic predictor of treatment response.

finding: Among 97 experienced practitioners, a Sudarshan Kriya Yoga retreat was associated with changes in inflammatory and antioxidant gene-expression measures, including IL6, relative to a comparison group.
limitation: Allocation was not random, and pre-pandemic and pandemic-era cohorts differed. The intervention combined breathing and meditation; it does not isolate mantra or establish general clinical benefit.

finding: A three-week retreat study comparing 28 experienced meditators with 34 community-based practitioners reported changes in TNF and chromatin-related blood gene-expression patterns.
limitation: Retreat participation was not randomised. Lifestyle, setting and participant selection remain plausible explanations; molecular changes do not demonstrate improved disease outcomes.

design: Secondary imaging and transcriptomic analysis of a randomized trial
finding: A 94-person subset of a meditation, yoga and education trial linked changes in brain connectivity with stress-related measures and inflammatory gene-regulation signals, informing hypotheses about mind-body pathways.
limitation: This is a secondary analysis of NCT01308970, also represented by PMID 41020112 in the library. Associations between connectivity and molecular measures do not establish causal mediation or an independent trial replication.

finding: In 40 veterans with PTSD, Transcendental Meditation reduced clinician-rated symptoms more than usual care over 12 weeks. Half of the meditation group no longer met PTSD criteria, compared with 10% of controls.
limitation: A small pilot with usual-care comparison. Anger and quality of life did not differ significantly; this does not establish equivalence to trauma-focused psychotherapy.

finding: In 181 male prisoners, Transcendental Meditation reduced self-reported trauma symptoms and perceived stress relative to usual care after four months.
limitation: The control did not match instructor attention. Self-reported trauma symptoms are distinct from independently confirmed PTSD remission, and findings do not establish an effect on reoffending.

finding: Among 304 Black adults stratified by baseline blood pressure, meditation reduced systolic pressure by approximately 3.3 mmHg relative to health education in the high-normal-pressure group.
limitation: The benefit did not extend to the normal-pressure group or diastolic pressure. Hypertension-event differences were not significant, so the result is subgroup- and endpoint-specific.

finding: A 104-nurse trial across three hospitals reported improved wellbeing and lower burnout, anxiety and PTSD symptoms after Transcendental Meditation compared with delayed instruction.
limitation: The waitlist comparison leaves attention and expectancy effects unresolved. Outcomes were self-reported over three months; effects on patient care were not established.

finding: In 199 women living in poverty in Uganda, three months of Transcendental Meditation reduced perceived stress, anger and fatigue and improved self-efficacy and sleep quality relative to waitlist.
limitation: The trial relied on self-report and a waitlist comparator. Later reports of improved relationships or responses to domestic violence are not evidence that meditation prevents violence.

finding: In 114 rural Lebanese women, three months of Transcendental Meditation improved stress, happiness, resilience and self-efficacy relative to the comparison group.
limitation: Short follow-up and self-reported outcomes limit generalisation. Replication with longer follow-up and appraisal of investigator affiliations are important for assessing confidence.

finding: In 96 school-district staff, Transcendental Meditation improved mood and distress relative to waitlist over four months. An EEG subset of 79 participants also showed changes in the study's Brain Integration Scale.
limitation: The EEG composite is a study-specific measure, not proof of globally improved brain function. A waitlist does not isolate practice-specific effects from support and expectancy.

finding: In 2,182 NHS staff, a digital mindfulness app produced a small but statistically significant reduction in stress relative to an active digital control over 4.5 months, with additional benefits on several wellbeing measures.
limitation: Effects were small and burnout and sickness absence did not improve significantly. Engagement was limited; this supports a scalable adjunct rather than a substitute for organisational support.

finding: In 1,458 employees, an eight-week digital meditation programme improved perceived stress relative to waitlist, with an effect size of 0.85 at eight weeks and 0.71 at four months.
limitation: Participants volunteered, most were women, and the comparator did not match attention. Greater use correlated with improvement but was not itself randomised.

finding: In 1,281 adults with substantial psychological distress, an eight-week hybrid digital mindfulness programme plus usual services reduced distress more than usual services alone, with an effect size of approximately 0.53.
limitation: Follow-up ended at eight weeks, and economic estimates reflect the trial's Chinese service context. Longer-term durability and transfer to other settings remain untested.
